newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: East Timor bishop says human rights still a problem.
newsitem.headline: East Timor bishop says human rights still a problem.

text.p: The new Catholic bishop in the troubled territory of East Timor said on Tuesday that human rights had improved in the area but the matter remained a problem.

Bishop Basilio Do Nascimento, who will be installed on Wednesday to head the newly created diocese of Baucau, told Reuters the situation in East Timor was "catastrophic" in the mid 1970s when Indonesia annexed the former Portuguese colony.
"When I came here the situation was changed. It is not so hard now".
Asked if East Timor could be granted more autonomy by Jakarta, Do Nascimento said "in some years maybe".
Do Nascimento, 46, will head a diocese numbering 300,000 out of East Timor's 800,000 people.

Pope John Paul split the church administration of the former Portuguese colony late last year and named Bishop Basilio Do Nascimento to head the newly created diocese of Baucau covering the eastern end of East Timor.
Welcome arches were put up in Baucau, a town of about 100,000, nestled between hills on three sides and the sea on the other, in the bishop's honour.
Do Nascimento, who left East Timor in 1959 and spent 25 years in Europe before returning in 1994, wore a white cassock with red buttons and red lining, and a silver cross around his neck.

There was a procession of hundreds of people including bare-chested local tribesmen wearing decorated sarongs and red bandannas, who waved machetes as they danced in the street. But there were no signs of the Indonesian army or any security forces in the town, whose cathedral was brightly lit with coloured lights.

The Roman Catholic administration in East Timor comes under the Pope rather than part of the Indonesian church establishment. Thus, papal nuncio Monseigneur Pietro Sambi, the Vatican's ambassador, will install the new bishop at a ceremony at Baucau on Wednesday.
The territory's other bishop, popular Nobel peace laureate Carlos Belo, has said dividing the diocese into two would not split the Timorese, but enhance their faith.

The U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for democracy, human rights and labour, John Shattuck, is due to visit Dili on Thursday and Friday. He will be followed over the weekend by U.N. special envoy Jamsheed Marker, diplomatic sources said.
Reuters television correspondent Sarni Ocampo reported from the East Timor capital Dili that all was normal on Tuesday.
"There is no unusual activity, no extra security," he said.

Some diplomats in Jakarta said East Timorese might stage demonstrations over the next few days with the presence of more than two dozen journalists from foreign news organisations allowed by the government to cover the bishop's installation.
Indonesia invaded the territory on December 7, 1975, after civil war broke out following the withdrawal of Portuguese colonial authorities.
Jakarta incorporated it into Indonesia as its 27th province in July, 1976 in a move not recognised by the United Nations.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said on Tuesday he had discussed human rights issues and East Timor with Shattuck, who arrived in Jakarta on Sunday. Diplomatic sources said the trip, Shattuck's first since 1995, was not unusual.
Marker, the U.N. special envoy, has said he would decide how to proceed over East Timor after visiting Portugal and Indonesia.
He said in Lisbon earlier this month he was optimistic over negotiations between Portugal and Indonesia, which have dragged on for almost 15 years.
